track.name: data
track.label: Data & Analytics
track.summary: Learn the core toolkit of a data analyst — turning raw, messy data into clear answers and visuals that drive real decisions — through the analytics process, SQL, statistics, and data visualization.

phases.title: The Analytics Process & Thinking with Data
phases.description: The mindset and process analysts use to turn a business question into a decision — asking, preparing, processing, analyzing, and sharing.

phases.title: SQL Fundamentals
phases.description: Query, filter, join, and summarize data directly in a database — the single most in-demand analyst skill.

phases.title: Data Cleaning & Preparation
phases.description: Real data is messy — find and fix missing values, duplicates, and type problems before you trust any analysis built on it.

phases.title: Statistics for Analysts
phases.description: The statistical thinking behind every dashboard and report — describing data, understanding distributions, and not mistaking correlation for causation.

phases.title: Data Visualization & Dashboards
phases.description: Turn analysis into charts and dashboards that someone else can understand and act on in seconds.

phases.title: Intro to Python for Data Analysis
phases.description: Python and pandas basics for when a spreadsheet or SQL query isn't enough — loading, wrangling, and exploring data in code.

phases.title: Geospatial Analytics & Location Intelligence
phases.description: Location intelligence for real business decisions — reading and mapping geospatial data in Python, the GIS platforms analysts actually reach for, and applied predictive modeling for retail site selection and store-footprint optimization.

topics.title: The Analytics Process: Ask, Prepare, Process, Analyze, Share
topics.description: The six-phase framework analysts use to structure any project, from defining the problem to acting on the results.

steps.d: Take a vague request ('improve our sales') and rewrite it as a specific, measurable question ('which product category has the highest churn rate, and why?').
List the tables, date ranges, and metrics required to answer your question — sales, churn, product category — and verify those fields exist.
Remove duplicates, handle nulls, check data types, and validate that the final dataset matches what you need before analysis.
Calculate mean, median, percentiles, and variance for your key metrics to understand the baseline distribution.
Write a one-paragraph summary of your results for a non-technical manager, naming the specific insight and its business implication.

topics.title: Asking Effective Questions & Data-Driven Decisions
topics.description: How to turn a vague business problem into a specific, answerable question before you touch any data.

steps.d: Take a statement like 'we need to understand customer behavior' and convert it into a specific, answerable question with a clear success metric.
Name what you are testing (pricing strategy) and what you are measuring (conversion rate), and explain why you expect a relationship.
Set the time period, customer segment, and data sources for your analysis — decide whether you need all data or a representative sample.
List other variables that might explain your result (seasonality, competitive activity, external events) and plan how you'll isolate the effect you care about.

steps.t: Validate that your question is answerable
steps.d: Check whether the data exists, is clean enough, and is recent enough to give you a trustworthy answer within your timeline.

topics.title: SQL SELECT & Filtering Basics
topics.description: Write your first queries — selecting columns, filtering rows, and sorting results.

steps.t: Write a SELECT with multiple columns
steps.d: Query a table and choose specific columns (SELECT customer_id, order_date, amount) instead of fetching the entire table.
Add WHERE clauses to show only orders over $100, or transactions in the past 30 days, or records matching a specific customer.
Arrange your result set by descending revenue or ascending date, and use LIMIT to return only the top 10 or 100 rows.
Write WHERE with AND and OR operators to filter for orders placed after Q3 2024 AND with a status of 'shipped' OR 'delivered'.
Check that your result has the right number of rows and columns, and spot-check a few values against the source data to confirm correctness.

topics.title: JOINs — Combining Tables
topics.description: Combine rows from two or more tables using INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, and FULL JOINs.

steps.t: Write an INNER JOIN on a shared key
steps.d: Combine a customers table with an orders table using INNER JOIN ON customers.id = orders.customer_id to match each order to its customer.
Run the same query with LEFT JOIN and compare the row count — LEFT JOIN preserves all customers even if they have no orders, while INNER JOIN does not.
Write a query that chains JOINs to pull customer name, order date, and product name from customers, orders, and products tables.

steps.t: Handle NULL values in a join
steps.d: Add WHERE clauses or COALESCE to deal with rows where the join key is NULL or missing, and verify your row count matches expectations.
Check that the row count and values match what you expect by comparing the joined result to the original tables, and verify no duplicates were created.

topics.title: Aggregating Data with GROUP BY
topics.description: Collapse rows into summaries with GROUP BY and aggregate functions like COUNT, SUM, and AVG.

steps.t: Write a basic GROUP BY query
steps.d: Collapse rows by customer or month using GROUP BY and COUNT to answer how many orders each customer placed.

steps.t: Combine GROUP BY with aggregate functions
steps.d: Use SUM to total revenue by region, AVG to calculate mean order value by product, and COUNT DISTINCT to count unique customers.

steps.t: Add a HAVING clause to filter groups
steps.d: Write a query that shows only customer segments with total spending above $10,000, or regions with more than 100 orders.
Write a GROUP BY on both product_category AND month to see revenue per category over time in a single result.
Sum the aggregated values back up to check they match the total in the base table, and verify that row count makes sense.

topics.title: Data Quality & Common Cleaning Tasks
topics.description: Spot the data quality problems — wrong types, inconsistent formatting, outliers — that break an analysis before it starts.

steps.t: Audit data types in a table
steps.d: Run a query to check whether dates are stored as text instead of DATE type, or money values are strings instead of numbers.
Compute MIN, MAX, and percentiles (P10, P90) for numeric columns to identify whether -$50,000 orders or age=999 values are real or data errors.
Look for state abbreviations stored as 'CA' in some rows and 'California' in others, or phone numbers with and without hyphens.
Write a query that shows how many NULLs, empty strings, and missing values exist in each column, and note which are acceptable.
Report the percentage of rows with data problems (wrong types, inconsistency, extremes) and decide whether the dataset is usable for analysis.

topics.title: Handling Missing Data & Duplicates
topics.description: Decide when to drop, fill, or flag missing values, and how to find and remove duplicate records.

steps.d: Write a query using ROW_NUMBER to identify whether the same customer_id appears multiple times, and decide whether to keep, merge, or drop duplicates.
For a nullable column, decide whether to drop rows with NULLs, fill them with a default value like 0 or 'Unknown', or flag them separately.
Write a query that uses CASE or COALESCE to replace missing state abbreviations with the most common state, or missing amounts with the average order value.
Apply your deduplication logic (keep first occurrence, or aggregate duplicates), then verify the row count dropped as expected.
Record how many rows you dropped for each reason, which columns you filled, and what values you used so others can reproduce your work.

topics.title: Descriptive Statistics — Center & Spread
topics.description: Summarize a dataset with mean, median, mode, and standard deviation before drawing any conclusions from it.

steps.d: Calculate the average order value and the median price, and note which one better represents a typical transaction if there are extreme outliers.
Measure the spread in your data — a small standard deviation means values cluster near the mean, a large one means they are scattered.
Identify the most common value (mode), the 25th percentile (Q1), the 75th percentile (Q3), and the interquartile range to describe the middle 50% of your data.
Explain what a 15% coefficient of variation (SD/mean) means for revenue stability, and how that compares to industry benchmarks if available.
Spot-check your descriptive statistics by sorting the data and visually confirming that the median and quartiles fall where your calculations said they should.

topics.title: Understanding Distributions
topics.description: Recognize the shape of your data — normal, skewed, uniform — and why that shape changes which statistics you can trust.

steps.d: Plot the distribution of a numeric column (revenue, age, transaction amount) to see whether data clusters at one end or spreads evenly.
Describe whether your distribution is left-skewed (tail on the left), right-skewed (tail on the right), or roughly symmetric.
Check whether the histogram looks bell-shaped, and compare your data to a theoretical normal distribution with the same mean and SD.

steps.t: Recognize when to use different statistics
steps.d: Explain why the median is better than mean for a right-skewed distribution (like customer lifetime value), and when the mean is appropriate.

steps.t: Choose a test based on distribution shape
steps.d: Decide whether to use a t-test (assumes normal distribution) or a non-parametric test based on what your histogram and Q-Q plot tell you about normality.

topics.title: Correlation vs. Causation
topics.description: Why two variables moving together doesn't mean one causes the other, and how to avoid that trap in your own analysis.

steps.d: Compute Pearson's r between two variables (marketing spend and revenue) and note whether the correlation is strong, weak, or zero.

steps.t: Visualize correlation with a scatter plot
steps.d: Plot two variables against each other and describe the pattern — does revenue follow a line (correlation), or scatter randomly (no relationship)?
Find two variables that move together (ice cream sales and drowning deaths) and explain an alternative cause (both spike in summer) without claiming one causes the other.
When two metrics correlate, list other factors that might explain both (time of year, competitor activity, marketing spend) before concluding causation.

steps.t: Distinguish correlation from causation in reporting
steps.d: Rewrite an analysis that claims 'ad spend causes revenue growth' to say 'ad spend and revenue are correlated; we need an experiment to test causation'.

topics.title: Choosing the Right Chart
topics.description: Match a chart type to the question you're answering instead of defaulting to whatever your tool suggests first.

steps.t: Match chart type to your question
steps.d: For 'which region had the highest revenue?', choose a bar chart; for 'how did revenue change over time?', choose a line chart; for 'what percent of sales is each category?', choose a pie or stacked bar.
When your tool suggests a chart, verify that the axes start at zero (for bar charts) or that you are not truncating a small change to make it look large.

steps.t: Choose between categorical and continuous axes
steps.d: Use a bar chart for discrete categories (regions, products) and a line chart for continuous time series (daily sales, monthly growth).

steps.t: Test chart clarity with a peer
steps.d: Show your chart to someone unfamiliar with the data and ask what story it tells in 10 seconds — if they can't answer, redesign it.

steps.t: Build the same data in three formats
steps.d: Create the same result as a table, a bar chart, and a line chart, then present the one that makes the insight fastest to see.

topics.title: Dashboard Design Principles
topics.description: Layout, hierarchy, and focus — the design choices that make a dashboard readable in five seconds instead of five minutes.

steps.t: Establish hierarchy with size and position
steps.d: Place your most important metric in the top-left, use larger fonts for headline numbers, and group related elements visually.
Use a single color for one metric, red/green sparingly for variance (bad/good), and a consistent palette across all dashboards so users know what to expect.
Remove gridlines, unused axis labels, and legends for single-series charts; limit the number of metrics per dashboard to five or eight.
Show not just 'Revenue: $2M' but also 'Revenue: $2M (up 15% vs last month)', so viewers can instantly judge performance.

steps.t: Design for scanning in five seconds
steps.d: Arrange your dashboard so a busy executive can land on the headline metric, understand the trend, and spot any red flags without reading text.

topics.title: Building Dashboards with Free BI Tools
topics.description: Hands-on practice building an interactive dashboard in a free tool like Looker Studio or Tableau Public.

steps.d: Create a free Looker Studio or Tableau Public account and connect it to a sample dataset (Google Sheets, CSV, or public data) so you can start building.
Add at least one table, one chart, and one filter (by date or category) so the dashboard updates when the user changes the filter.
Connect your dashboard to a live source so it updates daily or weekly without manual copy-paste, and verify the refresh happened by checking a date field.
Set up a click path so clicking on a region shows detailed metrics for that region, or clicking on a date range recalculates summary stats.
Publish your dashboard to a shareable link, ask a peer for feedback on clarity and usefulness, and refine based on what they say they see and understand.

topics.title: Python Basics for Data Analysis
topics.description: Enough Python syntax — variables, loops, functions — to start automating the analysis work a spreadsheet can't.

steps.d: Write code that creates variables for an order amount, a tax rate, and a date, and verify Python recognizes them as int, float, and string respectively.

steps.t: Write a for loop over data
steps.d: Loop through a list of order amounts and print each one, or calculate the running total by accumulating values across iterations.
Write an if-elif-else that marks orders over $100 as 'large' and under $10 as 'small', and test it against a sample dataset.
Define a function that takes an order amount and tax rate as inputs and returns the total including tax; call it multiple times with different values.
Add comments explaining what each line does, then have a peer read your code without the original description and confirm they understand it.

topics.title: Pandas Fundamentals
topics.description: Load, index, filter, and summarize tabular data with pandas DataFrames, the workhorse of Python data analysis.

steps.t: Load a CSV into a pandas DataFrame
steps.d: Read a CSV file into a DataFrame using pd.read_csv(), then print the shape, columns, and first five rows to confirm the data loaded correctly.
Create a filtered DataFrame that shows only rows where revenue > $1000, or where product_category == 'Electronics'.

steps.t: Aggregate data with groupby and sum
steps.d: Group revenue by region using groupby('region').sum(), then by month using groupby(pd.Grouper(freq='M')).sum() to see totals by time.
Sort a DataFrame by revenue in descending order, then add a rank column using rank() to number rows 1, 2, 3 within each group.
Check that the sum of grouped values equals the original total, and that row counts make sense after filtering and grouping.

topics.title: Exploratory Data Analysis with Pandas
topics.description: Combine pandas with basic plotting to explore a new dataset and spot patterns before formal analysis begins.

steps.d: Use describe() to compute mean, std, min, max for all numeric columns at once, then focus on columns with unexpected ranges.
Create histograms for revenue, order count, and customer age using df.hist() to spot outliers and understand which values are typical.
Compute a correlation matrix with df.corr() and identify which pairs of metrics move together (correlation > 0.7 or < -0.7).
Use df.isnull().sum() to count NULLs per column and df.duplicated().sum() to count exact duplicates, then decide how to handle them.
Write a short summary of your findings (highest-revenue region, most common product, churn rate) with the exact metrics you calculated and what they imply.

topics.title: Geospatial Data & Python — GeoPandas, Shapefiles & Mapping Fundamentals
topics.description: What geospatial (vector) data actually is, and how to read, manipulate, and map shapefiles and GeoJSON with geopandas — including basic spatial joins.

steps.d: Use gpd.read_file() to load a shapefile of state boundaries or city polygons, and verify the geometry column contains polygon or point objects.

steps.t: Project coordinates to a common system
steps.d: Transform your geodata from WGS84 (lat/lon) to a projected CRS like EPSG:3857 so you can calculate distance and area accurately.
Use gpd.sjoin() to join a points table (customer locations) with a polygons table (sales regions) to find which region each customer belongs to.
Compute the distance from each store location to a competitor using distance() or create a buffer zone around hospitals using buffer().

steps.t: Map a choropleth to visualize geographic data
steps.d: Color-code regions by revenue or population density using gdf.plot(column='revenue', legend=True) to identify hot and cold spots spatially.

topics.title: GIS Visualization Platforms — ArcGIS, QGIS, CARTO & Alteryx
topics.description: What each tool in a location-analytics stack is actually for — desktop GIS mapping in ArcGIS/QGIS, cloud-based dashboards in CARTO, and no-code data prep with built-in predictive modeling in Alteryx.

steps.d: Build a table listing ArcGIS, QGIS, CARTO, and Alteryx with their key features (layer-based mapping, interactive dashboards, SQL-based, no-code data prep) so you can see which tool fits each use case.
Download QGIS, load a shapefile or GeoJSON, apply a color ramp by a data attribute, and export the map as an image or interactive file.

steps.t: Build a cloud dashboard in CARTO
steps.d: Create a CARTO account, upload a CSV with coordinates, build an interactive map layer, and add a control that filters by a category.
List what each tool (ArcGIS, QGIS, CARTO, Alteryx) is best for — desktop analysis vs. publishing dashboards vs. no-code data prep — and pick one for your use case.
Choose which tools you'll use for a retail analysis project (QGIS for exploration, CARTO for publishing, Alteryx for prep) and justify each choice.

topics.title: Location Analytics in Practice — Retail Site Selection, Store Footprint & Applied Predictive Modeling
topics.description: How consulting and advisory firms actually use this toolkit — retail site-selection and store-footprint optimization, using Gradient Boosting and Random Forest to predict foot traffic and demand.

steps.d: Collect foot traffic data (from mobile or sensor data providers) and demographic data (census, third-party) for candidate retail locations.
Create variables like 'distance to transit', 'competitor density', 'median income within 1km', and 'weekend foot traffic' to use as inputs to a model.

steps.t: Train a Random Forest or Gradient Boosting model
steps.d: Use scikit-learn or XGBoost to fit a model that predicts foot traffic from location features, and evaluate it on hold-out stores.
Identify which features the model ranks highest (e.g., 'competitor density' explains 40% of variance), and explain why that matters for site selection.
Apply your trained model to score proposed new store locations and recommend the top 3 based on predicted foot traffic and profitability.
